findings.title: RSA-based JWT/JOSE algorithm is broken by Shor's algorithm
findings.message: A JWT or JOSE object is signed (RS256/384/512, PS256/384/512) or encrypted (RSA-OAEP, RSA1_5) with RSA. Shor's algorithm recovers the RSA private key from the public key, which is usually published in a JWKS endpoint: anyone could then mint valid tokens for your users, and encrypted tokens recorded today could be opened later.
findings.suggestion: Plan the move to post-quantum JOSE algorithms: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for token signatures (standardized for JOSE in RFC 9964: ML-DSA-44, -65, -87), and ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for encrypted tokens. Tokens are short-lived, so the urgent part is the signing key and the verifiers: make them algorithm-agile (publish several keys in the JWKS, pin the accepted algorithms per key) so issuers can switch without a flag day. RSA1_5 should be removed today regardless; it is vulnerable to padding-oracle attacks.

findings.title: RSA is broken by Shor's algorithm
findings.message: RSA key generation, encryption or signing detected. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm recovers RSA private keys, and data encrypted today can be harvested now and decrypted later.
findings.suggestion: Plan a protocol migration, not a drop-in swap. For key establishment and encryption, move to ML-KEM (FIPS 203); for signatures, move to ML-DSA (FIPS 204). During the transition, a hybrid scheme (e.g. X25519+ML-KEM, or RSA/ECDSA dual signatures with ML-DSA) keeps classical security while adding post-quantum protection.

findings.title: ECDSA-based JWT algorithm is forgeable with Shor's algorithm
findings.message: A JWT or JOSE object is signed with ECDSA (ES256, ES256K, ES384, ES512). Shor's algorithm recovers the private key from the public key, which is usually published in a JWKS endpoint, so a quantum attacker could mint valid tokens for any user.
findings.suggestion: Plan the move to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) token signatures, standardized for JOSE in RFC 9964 (`ML-DSA-44`, `ML-DSA-65`, `ML-DSA-87`). ML-DSA signatures are around 2.4 to 4.6 KB against 64 to 132 bytes for ECDSA, so check header size limits on proxies and cookies. Make verifiers algorithm-agile now (several keys in the JWKS, accepted algorithms pinned per key) so issuers can switch without a flag day.

findings.title: SHA-1 is broken classically and weakened further by quantum search
findings.message: SHA-1 used as a hash or inside a signature detected. Practical SHA-1 collisions have been public since 2017 (SHAttered) and chosen-prefix collisions since 2020, so it must not protect signatures, certificates or integrity checks today. Quantum search only widens the margin further. NIST plans to retire SHA-1 entirely by 2030.
findings.suggestion: Use SHA-256 or SHA-384 (SHA-2), or SHA3-256. No automatic fix is offered: digests are usually stored, compared or sent to other systems, so changing the algorithm silently would break existing values and interoperability. Migrate the data and its consumers together.

findings.title: Triple DES is deprecated and has too little margin against Grover's algorithm
findings.message: Triple DES (TDEA / DESede) detected. Its effective strength is at most 112 bits classically, Grover's algorithm shrinks that margin further, and its 64-bit block makes long sessions vulnerable to birthday attacks (Sweet32). NIST disallowed 3DES for encryption after 2023.
findings.suggestion: Use AES-256, preferably in an authenticated mode such as GCM. No automatic fix is offered: AES needs a different key size, IV length and block size, and data already encrypted with 3DES must be decrypted and re-encrypted.

findings.title: AES-128 keeps only about 64 bits of security against Grover's algorithm
findings.message: A 128-bit AES key detected. Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speed-up to brute-force key search, so AES-128 drops to roughly 64 bits of quantum security. NIST still accepts AES-128 today (it is the reference point for post-quantum security category 1), but long-lived secrets and frameworks such as NSA CNSA 2.0 call for AES-256.
findings.suggestion: Use 256-bit keys (AES-256). Unlike public-key migrations this is usually a parameter change: the API, the IV and the authentication tag stay the same. Keys already stored or shared with other systems must be re-generated and re-distributed, so plan a key rotation alongside the code change.

findings.title: ECDSA signatures are forgeable with Shor's algorithm
findings.message: ECDSA signing or verification detected. Shor's algorithm recovers the private key from a public key, which lets an attacker forge signatures. Long-lived trust anchors (firmware signing keys, root certificates, code-signing identities) are the most exposed, because they must stay valid for years.
findings.suggestion: Migrate signatures to ML-DSA (FIPS 204), or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) where a conservative hash-based scheme is preferred. ML-DSA keys and signatures are much larger than ECDSA ones, so check certificate sizes, wire formats and storage. During the transition, dual (composite) signatures with ECDSA and ML-DSA keep classical verifiers working.

findings.title: Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (including X25519/X448) is broken by Shor's algorithm
findings.message: Elliptic-curve key agreement detected (ECDH, ECMQV, ECIES or the Montgomery-curve variants X25519/X448). Shor's algorithm solves the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, so recorded key exchanges can be decrypted later (harvest now, decrypt later). X25519 is modern and well-implemented, but it is just as exposed to a quantum attacker.
findings.suggestion: Move key establishment to ML-KEM (FIPS 203). The recommended transition is a hybrid key exchange such as X25519MLKEM768 (already deployed in TLS 1.3 by major browsers and CDNs): both shared secrets feed the key schedule, so the connection stays secure if either algorithm holds. This changes the handshake, so it is a protocol migration, not a parameter swap.

findings.title: Elliptic-curve keys are broken by Shor's algorithm
findings.message: Generic elliptic-curve key material detected ("EC" key pairs, curve parameters). The same EC key can serve key agreement (ECDH) or signatures (ECDSA), and this call alone does not tell which, so it is reported on its own. Either way, Shor's algorithm recovers the private key from the public key. Where the file also performs the actual ECDH or ECDSA operation, that call gets its own, more specific finding.
findings.suggestion: Find out what these keys are used for. For key agreement or encryption, move to ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ideally through a hybrid such as X25519MLKEM768 during the transition. For signatures, move to ML-DSA (FIPS 204), possibly as a composite signature alongside ECDSA. Either way, this is a protocol migration, not a parameter swap.

findings.title: TLS cipher suites with classical key exchange are exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later
findings.message: TLS 1.2 cipher suites configured with RSA, DHE or ECDHE key exchange. All three rest on problems Shor's algorithm solves, so TLS traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a large quantum computer exists. Suites with static RSA key exchange (TLS_RSA_WITH_*) also lack forward secrecy: a single leaked server key opens every past session, even without a quantum computer.
findings.suggestion: Prefer TLS 1.3 and enable a hybrid post-quantum key exchange group such as X25519MLKEM768 wherever your TLS stack and peers support it, keeping a classical group as fallback during the transition. Hybrid key exchange protects recorded traffic now, without waiting for post-quantum certificates. Remove static RSA suites today.

findings.title: RSA is broken by Shor's algorithm
findings.message: An RSA key or certificate. Keys and certificates live for years, and whatever they protect or sign until they are replaced can be attacked later: a quantum computer running Shor's algorithm recovers the private key from the public one.
findings.suggestion: Plan a protocol migration, not a drop-in swap. For key establishment and encryption, move to ML-KEM (FIPS 203); for signatures, move to ML-DSA (FIPS 204). During the transition, a hybrid scheme (e.g. X25519+ML-KEM, or RSA/ECDSA dual signatures with ML-DSA) keeps classical security while adding post-quantum protection.
